title: Why Did Christianity Grow Differently in South Korea and Japan?
author: Natural experiment
focus: Two wealthy East Asian allies look surprisingly alike, until the religion numbers split wide open.
framing: Two nearby countries share a modern neighborhood, high development, deep ties to the United States, and long histories shaped by Buddhism and Confucian learning. So why did Christianity become much more common in South Korea than in Japan?

comparisonPoints.label: Modern development
comparisonPoints.detail: World Bank data puts Japan and South Korea close in 2025 GDP per person, at about $35,951 and $36,227.

comparisonPoints.label: Everyday modern life
comparisonPoints.detail: The World Bank reports similar life expectancy in 2024: about 84.0 years in Japan and 83.6 years in South Korea.

comparisonPoints.label: Postwar alliances
comparisonPoints.detail: The U.S. State Department describes both relationships as enduring security alliances.

reveal.label: The surprise
reveal.detail: Pew Research Center's 2023 East Asia survey found 32% of South Korean adults identify as Christian, compared with 2% in Japan.

scriptParagraphs: Here is the mystery. Japan and South Korea are neighbors. Both are wealthy, high-tech democracies. Both became close allies of the United States after devastating wars.

According to the World Bank, their 2025 GDP per person was almost side by side: about thirty-five thousand nine hundred dollars in Japan and thirty-six thousand two hundred dollars in South Korea. Their life expectancy is close too.
So we have to ask the learning question: are these two countries comparable enough that a big difference should make us curious?

Pew Research Center found that in a 2023 survey, thirty-two percent of South Korean adults identified as Christian. In Japan, it was two percent. That is about one out of three adults in South Korea, compared with about one out of fifty in Japan.
Hmm. Interesting.

The easy guesses do not quite work. It is not just America, because America was deeply connected to both countries. It is not just wealth and technology, because both countries are highly developed. It is not simply East Asia resisting Christianity, because South Korea does not fit that story.
So we look for what Christianity seemed to be attached to in each place.

In Japan, Christianity arrived early and grew for a while. Then the Tokugawa shogunate, the warrior government that ruled Japan for more than two hundred years, treated it as dangerous. Christianity was banned. Christians had to hide. Imagine if joining a church made your family look like it was helping a foreign enemy.

In Korea, Protestant missionaries later became connected not only with preaching, but also with schools, hospitals, reading, women's education, and modern medicine. And when Korea was ruled by Japan, some Christian institutions could feel like places to learn, organize, and keep a little room to breathe.
So the difference is not that one people was naturally this way and another people was naturally that way. It is about what the same religion came wearing.
In one place: danger sign. In another place: schoolbag, hospital bag, and sometimes a flag of resistance.
The final question is: when a new idea arrives somewhere, what does it look like to the people opening the door?

title: Why Did New York Grow Around Trains While Los Angeles Grew Around Cars?
author: Natural experiment
focus: Two giant American metro areas look like peers, until the commute numbers reveal two different city skeletons.
framing: New York and Los Angeles are both huge, rich, diverse U.S. metro areas, but one learned to gather around trains while the other learned to spread across roads, freeways, and many centers.

comparisonPoints.label: Giant coastal metros
comparisonPoints.detail: Census Reporter, using ACS 2024 data, puts the New York metro area at about 19.9 million people and the Los Angeles metro area at about 12.9 million.

comparisonPoints.label: High-income, high-cost regions
comparisonPoints.detail: ACS 2024 estimates put median household income near $99,900 in the New York metro and $96,400 in the Los Angeles metro, with owner-occupied home values far above the U.S. figure in both places.

comparisonPoints.label: Global gateway regions
comparisonPoints.detail: ACS 2024 estimates say foreign-born residents are about 30.8% of the New York metro and 33.4% of the Los Angeles metro.

reveal.label: The surprise
reveal.detail: ACS 2024 commute data shows about 27% of New York metro workers used public transportation, compared with about 3.5% in the Los Angeles metro. Inside the central cities, the split was about 49% in New York City and 6% in Los Angeles.

scriptParagraphs: Here is the mystery. New York and Los Angeles are both giant American metro areas. Both are coastal. Both are expensive. Both are full of immigrants, jobs, movies, money, music, languages, and people trying to get somewhere.

According to Census Reporter, using 2024 American Community Survey data, the New York metro area had about nineteen point nine million people. The Los Angeles metro had about twelve point nine million. Their median household incomes were not wildly far apart either: about ninety-nine thousand nine hundred dollars in the New York metro and ninety-six thousand four hundred in the Los Angeles metro.
So they belong in the same big-city conversation.

Then the reveal: in the New York metro, about twenty-seven percent of workers used public transportation to get to work. In the Los Angeles metro, it was about three and a half percent. Inside the central cities, the split was sharper: about forty-nine percent in New York City and about six percent in Los Angeles.
Hmm. Interesting.

The easy guesses do not quite work. It is not just weather. It is not just wealth. And it is definitely not that Los Angeles has no transit. LA Metro reported more than three hundred eleven million boardings in 2024, and its rail system now has more than one hundred miles of service.
So what happened?

New York became crowded early, before ordinary families owned cars. It had elevated trains in the 1800s. After the 1888 blizzard froze above-ground travel, the case for underground trains became stronger. The first official subway opened in 1904, and by 1915 the IRT reached every borough except Staten Island. The subway did not just serve neighborhoods. It helped make them.

Los Angeles had trains too. Streetcars were still strong in the 1920s. But LA grew explosively just as the automobile was becoming ordinary. The Los Angeles Public Library describes 1920s LA as one of the first truly car-centric cities: by 1925, there was one car for every three residents, twice the national average.

And LA was not built around only one center. It became a constellation: downtown, Hollywood, Wilshire, the ports, beach cities, studio towns, valleys, airports. Planners might call that polycentric. For kids, say this: instead of one giant magnet in the middle, LA had many magnets spread across the map.

Once homes, stores, studios, and jobs spread out, the car became the tool that connected the dots. Then roads and freeways made driving easier, which made spreading out easier, which made driving feel even more necessary.
So the answer is not that New Yorkers are train people and Angelenos are car people by nature. The old choices taught each city a habit.
The question to keep is: when a city is still choosing its bones, does it teach people to gather at stations or scatter toward parking lots?
